newsitem.title: USA: Wide U.S. August trade gap seen depressing Q3 GDP.
newsitem.headline: Wide U.S. August trade gap seen depressing Q3 GDP.

text.p: Despite a 6.6 percent narrowing in the August U.S. trade deficit, the gap remains wide and should act as a drag on third-quarter economic growth, economists said on Friday.
While the U.S. trade deficit in goods and services shrank to $10.83 billion in August from a revised $11.60 billion July gap, it was still substantially higher than forecast.

"It does have significant repercussions for third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) in the sense that net-exports are shaping up as a drag here," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc.
Economists polled by Reuters expected the August gap to narrow to $8.5 billion.
Some analysts said they were puzzled at July's huge deficit, the widest in eight and a half years, after the robust economic growth coming out of the second quarter.
The Commerce Department revised the July deficit down to $11.6 billion, but the figure was still too close to the originally reported $11.68 billion for comfort.
Even though U.S. exports bounced back in August, they failed to completely recoup July's sizable 3.6 percent drop.
"They bounced back 3.0 percent after falling in July. So we're still below June's level on exports, and imports grew modestly," said Mickey Levy, chief economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc.

The 1.6 percent jump in August imports followed a 1.2 percent rise in July. Some economists suggested that the demand for imported goods may be a spill-over effect from strong 4.7 percent economic growth in the second quarter.
The persistent strength of imports underscores the deterioration of net exports, which should prompt downward revisions to third quarter GDP forecasts, economists said.
"We had been below 2.0 percent in economic growth in the third quarter. Now we're close to one-and-a-half to one-and- three-quarters," said Levy.
On a bilateral trade basis, there was some narrowing of the U.S. trade deficit with Japan and a 63.2 percent drop in the gap with Western Europe. But the deficit with China ballooned 23 percent.
"You have significant widening of the bilateral deficit with China and that is preventing the (overall) deficit from improving much," said Karydakis of First Chicago.
The key point for the markets is that lower third quarter growth forecasts should fuel speculation that interest rates will fall, analysts said.
"It seems to have helped the bond market, and anything that helps the bond market seems to help the stock market," said Cynthia Latta, senior financial economist at DRI/McGraw Hill.
